look_here_first: OZARKGRASS: find a slender annual tuft with fibrous roots and a relatively NARROW, sometimes slightly nodding spring panicle. At 10–20× inspect ONE ~3–4 mm spikelet: TWO stiff nearly equal glumes enclose ONE fertile floret. The lemma has TWO small apical teeth; its SINGLE 8–12 mm often bent and twisted awn emerges BETWEEN those teeth. A true 1–2 mm membranous, minutely jagged ligule sits inside the blade–sheath junction. Flowerhead silhouette alone is not a confirmed ID; the current photo does NOT prove lemma teeth or ligule.

best_field_traits: Cool-season ANNUAL, usually 20–60 cm; fibrous rooted, solitary or small tuft, lacking stolons/rhizomes.
Leaves flat and variably hairy, sheaths open, auricles absent; 1–2 mm ragged-edged MEMBRANOUS ligule inside leaf collar.
Slender relatively NARROW panicle with ascending small branches; often appears gently bent or nodding at the tip.
Each ~3–4 mm spikelet contains ONE fertile floret enclosed by TWO firm nearly equal glumes.
Fertile lemma tip has TWO short teeth and ONE often bent/twisted ~8–12 mm awn emerging from the NOTCH between them; verify at 10–20×.
Annual habit, spring bloom or habitat are useful support only; photographs of panicle silhouette alone are NOT species confirmation.
what_to_photograph_for_confirmation: WHOLE ROOTED PLANT: a connected fibrous-rooted tuft with entire narrow seedhead in frame and a 1-cm scale; no stolons or rhizomes.
WHOLE PANICLE: side view from flag leaf through narrowly ascending, sometimes nodding flowering branches with attached mature spikelets.
SPIKELET 10–20×: TWO stiff, subequal, ~3–4 mm glumes surrounding ONE fertile floret, mm ruler for scale.
CRITICAL LEMMA 20×: clearly show two terminal teeth and exactly ONE ~8–12 mm bent/twisted awn originating in notch BETWEEN those teeth.
LEAF COLLAR: turn back the blade and show the actual 1–2 mm ragged-edged membranous ligule with a 1-mm scale.
MATCHED LOOKALIKES: same-scale threeawn three-limbed lemma, lovegrass multifloret spikelet and panicgrass two-floret spikelet.
crew_field_check: OZARKGRASS: find a slender annual tuft with fibrous roots and a relatively NARROW, sometimes slightly nodding spring panicle. At 10–20× inspect ONE ~3–4 mm spikelet: TWO stiff nearly equal glumes enclose ONE fertile floret. The lemma has TWO small apical teeth; its SINGLE 8–12 mm often bent and twisted awn emerges BETWEEN those teeth. A true 1–2 mm membranous, minutely jagged ligule sits inside the blade–sheath junction. Flowerhead silhouette alone is not a confirmed ID; the current photo does NOT prove lemma teeth or ligule.

Aristida threeawns: normally THREE awn limbs arising from ONE lemma, vs Limnodea's single notched-lemma awn. Eragrostis lovegrasses: generally MULTIPLE florets per spikelet, not just one. Panicum (e.g., switchgrass): typically a lower sterile/staminate floret with a hardened fertile UPPER floret rather than one fertile floret with the Limnodea notched awn. Muhlenbergia: can ALSO have one fertile floret, so compare the paired glumes, lemma teeth/awn origin, ligule and annual tuft; panicle openness and one awn alone are insufficient.
Do not call a one-floret airy panicle Limnodea if you cannot see its paired glumes and two-toothed awned lemma. Label provisional grass sp. and collect flowering macro.

field_id_finish_pass.crew_teaching_summary: OZARKGRASS: a slender cool-season ANNUAL with a narrow flowering panicle and slender often curved single awns; confirmed species ID requires a 3–4 mm one-flowered spikelet, two subequal glumes, and a lemma whose ONE awn inserts BETWEEN TWO apical teeth. Current 11 archived exact-species photographs show habit, flowering heads, long awns, a separate basal root strand, and actual collar junction photographs, but do NOT prove a continuous rooted plant, a measured true inner 1–2 mm ligule or the critical small tooth/awn-origin macro. Compare Aristida's three awn limbs and multiflowered Eragrostis only through independently labelled look-alike panels.

Panicum (e.g., switchgrass): typically a lower sterile/staminate floret with a hardened fertile UPPER floret rather than one fertile floret with the Limnodea notched awn. Muhlenbergia: can ALSO have one fertile floret, so compare the paired glumes, lemma teeth/awn origin, ligule and annual tuft; panicle openness and one awn alone are insufficient.

measured_diagnostic_key_20261023.look_here_first: Small fibrous-rooted annual with slender contracted panicle; dissect one 3.5–4 mm spikelet. Two stiff subequal glumes enclose a single fertile floret whose TWO-toothed lemma bears ONE often bent awn arising between the teeth.
measured_diagnostic_key_20261023.growth_form_collar: Annual, approximately 20–60 cm, with no perennial rhizome or rooting stolon; true ligule a short, non-hair-fringed membranous flap, locally reported ~1–2 mm. Confirm exact attached blade/sheath junction.
measured_diagnostic_key_20261023.spikelet_glumes: Spikelets approximately 3.5–4 mm with one fertile floret and barren rachilla extension. Both stiff, rough, nearly equal glumes generally 3–5-veined and reaching the floret tip (GrassBase genus account). Count veins under transmitted light.
measured_diagnostic_key_20261023.lemma_palea_awn: Three-veined, keeled fertile lemma with two apical teeth; one subapical often bent/twisted awn arises from between teeth (regional accounts ~5–12 mm). Palea about 0.7× lemma length. Do not mislabel the awn as a glume awn.
measured_diagnostic_key_20261023.local_lookalikes: Aristida has three awn limbs on one lemma; Eragrostis usually several fertile florets per spikelet; Panicum has a lower sterile/staminate floret and hard upper fertile floret; Muhlenbergia can also be one-flowered, so inspect teeth, glume vein counts and awn insertion.

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 01 · LOOK HERE FIRST
field_id_short_tiles.short: Narrow spring panicle; one-flowered spikelet with one bent awn
field_id_short_tiles.details: SEE the actual same-species flowering panicles in panels 1,3,9–10 (indices 0,2,8,9). Ozarkgrass is an annual with a usually narrow, sometimes nodding spring panicle and one-flowered spikelets; only the published key—not these images—establishes two near-equal glumes, the apical lemma teeth and single awn between them. Do not use lovegrass/threeawn comparison photographs as though they were Ozarkgrass.
field_id_short_tiles.status: FIELD-READY SPRING PANICLE AND AWN CUE — SINGLE LEMMA-NOTCH MACRO MISSING

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 02 · TRACE THE ANNUAL BASE
field_id_short_tiles.short: Fibrous-rooted annual; panicle to ~12 cm in local treatment
field_id_short_tiles.details: Field habitat in panel 1 (index 0) shows green leafy shoots at the soil surface, NOT any exposed roots. Bob Harms' habit plate in panel 9 (index 8) includes a small basal root strand at the bottom of a separated left-hand culm; the central flowering panicle is on a different cut/laid stem. That does NOT prove an intact same-plant fibrous root crown plus flowering culm. To clear the gate, photograph one legally collected rooted individual upright in place, then dug with entire connected root system/crown/flowering head and a centimeter scale.
field_id_short_tiles.status: PARTIAL SEPARATE BASAL ROOT STRAND — CONNECTED ROOT-TO-FLOWERING PLANT STILL MISSING

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 03 · OPEN THE TRUE LIGULE
field_id_short_tiles.short: Membranous 1–2 mm; truncate and finely jagged
field_id_short_tiles.details: Actual exact-species blade–sheath junction photos are panel 4, Chet Burrier's full-size macro (index 3), and panel 14, Bob Harms' regional collar view (index 13). The Chet image shows pale projecting torn/ragged-looking junction tissue, not a fully opened inner membrane beside a millimeter bar. The Harms plate shows a photographed collar region, but no continuous clearly calibrated free ligule edge. Texas Hill Country key describes a 1–2 mm membranous, obtuse, lacerate ligule, glabrous collar, no auricles. Photograph the adaxial/INNER free edge with a ruler before claiming the length.
field_id_short_tiles.status: TWO REAL COLLAR PHOTOS — MEASURED INNER LIGULE STILL NEEDED

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 04 · COUNT AND MEASURE GLUMES
field_id_short_tiles.short: Two subequal awnless glumes, ~3–3.3 mm locally
field_id_short_tiles.details: Panels 2 and 11–12 (indices 1,10,11) show authentic Ozarkgrass awned flowering material. Neither proves both 3–5-veined glumes are separated and measured. The Williamson County treatment reports roughly 3–3.3 mm glumes; Kew GrassBase gives ~3.5–4 mm spikelets with one fertile floret and a barren rachilla extension. These are source measurements, NOT numbers derived from the images. Do not point glume arrows at uncertain scales in a cramped old source plate.
field_id_short_tiles.status: NEEDS_PUBLIC_PHOTO — TWO MEASURED GLUMES AND ONE FLORET

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 05 · FIND THE TWO-TOOTHED LEMMA
field_id_short_tiles.short: Lemma 2.7–2.9 mm; one 8–12.5 mm awn BETWEEN two teeth
field_id_short_tiles.details: Actual Limnodea awns appear in panels 2,5 and 11–12 (indices 1,4,10,11). Critical identification: the ONE awn emerges between TWO small teeth on a fertile lemma, not from a glume. Existing full-size photos do not isolate the two ~0.5-mm teeth at 20–40× with a mm reference, so gross awn arrows are okay but new tooth/awn-origin markers remain prohibited.
field_id_short_tiles.status: NEEDS_PUBLIC_PHOTO — LEMMA TEETH AND AWN INSERTION

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 06 · RULE OUT THREEAWNS AND LOVEGRASSES
field_id_short_tiles.short: One notched-lemma awn ≠ Aristida's three awn limbs
field_id_short_tiles.details: Three look-alike gallery panels are numbered 6,7,8 (indices 5,6,7): Aristida purpurea, Panicum virgatum and Eragrostis intermedia, respectively. None is a photograph of Limnodea. The Ozarkgrass reproductive comparison is panel 12 (index 11); one long awn alone is insufficient, because some Muhlenbergia also bear one. Confirm two-toothed lemma and glumes rather than confusing grass seeds or species images. Keep Joey Santore's individually licensed iNaturalist lovegrass photo on conditional NC terms only.
field_id_short_tiles.status: LOOK-ALIKE LESSON; MATCHED DISSECTED COMPARISONS MISSING

field_photo_quickcheck.heading: Ozarkgrass — expose the one lemma awn BETWEEN two teeth
steps: Species panels 1,3 and 9–10 show clump and narrow panicles. The Harms plate panel 9 (index 8) includes a separate root strand but lacks a fully connected flowering specimen; the CC0 field tuft panel 1 (index 0) does not expose roots.

True collar photos are Chet's visible pale junction (panel 4, index 3) and Bob Harms' collar region (panel 14, index 13). Open from the INSIDE and add a 1-mm ruler to show the actual free 1–2 mm lacerate ligule.
Panels 2,5,11–12 show long single awns (indices 1,4,10,11). Do not place a lemma-tooth arrow: the two ~0.5-mm teeth and insertion point are unconfirmed at pixel scale.

Panels 6–8 (indices 5–7) are Aristida/Panicum/Eragrostis look-alikes, not Limnodea. Aristida has a three-limbed awn; Eragrostis usually multiple florets/spikelet; Panicum typically two florets/spikelet.

Minimum closure photo set: same rooted + flowering specimen, exposed true ligule with 1mm bar, mature individual spikelet with both glumes, and 20–40× lemma showing one awn precisely BETWEEN two distinct teeth.
Retain credited CC BY-NC and Bob Harms sources conditionally pending exact image-level permissions. No new photographs or microscopic arrows installed.
field_photo_quickcheck.field_rule: NEVER certify a root-to-panicle connection, true ligule measurement, or 0.5 mm paired lemma teeth from photographs that do not show those structures plainly.
field_photo_quickcheck.warning: These photos teach recognition, not a Hays County native-range certification; final site rights-filtered deployment and mobile arrow QA are still unverified.
